newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: FLOODING CONTINUES IN NORTH WESTERN NSW
The town of Wee Waa in north-western New South Wales is expected to be isolated by floodwaters, after up to 180 millimetres of rain in the past two days.
Tamworth was virtually cut off by floodwaters overnight, and the entire suburb of Calala was isolated, with many people unable to get home.
Two people were rescued by floodboat when their car was stranded.
The water is now moving down the Peel and Namoi valleys.
The S-E-S has welcomed a break in the weather with no rainfall reported in the region overnight.
EUTHANASIA SURVEY FINDINGS RELEASED
A survey on euthanasia has found that almost one third of all Australian deaths were preceeded by a medical decision explicitly intended to hasten the patient's death.
They included four per-cent requested by the patient.
The survey is the first Australian study of treatments by doctors which could hasten a patient's death.
Tasmanian Liberal Senator Eric Abetz has released some of the findings ahead of the survey's publication in the Medical Journal of Australia next week.
Principal author, Professor Helga Kuhse, told a Senate inquiry the continued prohibition of voluntary euthanasia serves nobody well.
MINISTERS MEET OVER ROAD TOLL
National uniform driving laws and tougher penalties for some driving offences could be part of a package to be discussed by Transport ministers in Hobart today.
The package, aimed at delivering a quick improvement in Australia's road toll, may include stiffer penalties for drink driving, speeding and seat belt offences.
New South Wales, Queensland and the Federal Transport Minister, John Sharp asked for new safety measures to be considered at today's meeting after the national road toll rose 18 per cent last month.
It was the worst January road toll for five years.
HOWARD TO HOLD ROUND TABLE TALKS ON NATIVE TITLE
Prime Minister John Howard will hold roundtable discussions of Aboriginal, pastoral, and mining representatives today, to try and find common ground on native title.
It's the latest in a round of discussions on the High Court's Wik ruling, which found that native title can co-exist on pastoral leases.
Mr Howard says he's hopeful the meeting will provide the foundation for the development and consideration of issues in a constructive manner.
He hasn't ruled out options including legislating and amending the Racial discrimination Act.

Groups such as the Federal National Party and the National Farmers Federation have called for native title to be extinguished on pastoral leases, while Aboriginal groups have warned against taking such steps.
LIGHTERS TO BE CHILD RESISTANT
The Federal Government says from October, all disposable and novelty cigarette lighters must be child-resistant.
Import controls will ban the importation of such lighters after March next year.

The Consumer Affairs minister, Geoff Prosser, says in the past three years the deaths of nine children have been attributed to non child-resistant disposable cigarette lighters. He says many young children also suffer severe burns from playing with them.
Mr Prosser says fines for non-compliance will be up to 40-thousand dollars for individuals and 200-thousand dollars for a corporation.
